reading.title: Τέτταρες μῆνες μισθοῦ
reading.audioPlaceholder: Reading audio has not yet been recorded.
introduction: The troops’ unpaid wages connect the march to Epyaxa, wife of the Cilician ruler Syennesis. Her arrival, reported assistance, and subsequent negotiation give her a consequential place in the expedition.

Source: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.2.12–18 and 25–27. Xenophon marks both the financial gift and her request for a review as reports, while he states the payment of four months’ wages. The reading preserves that distinction. Its simple present-tense wording is adapted; it invents no speech, romantic motive, or private intention for Epyaxa. The later Tarsus continuation is explicitly compressed.

Blue glosses support names, passive/irregular verbs, reported-speech constructions, and untaught adjectives. Today’s targets concern noun forms, all/every/whole, quantities, and time. Money “for four months” is a quantity of wages, which we distinguish from an accusative duration expression.

reading.translation:
Cyrus owes the pay, and the soldiers repeatedly request the money. Then Epyaxa comes to Cyrus. The wife of Syennesis, the ruler of the Cilicians, travels with guards.

It is reported that Epyaxa provides Cyrus with much money. At that time Cyrus gives the army four months’ pay. The gift of money is a report, whereas the four months’ pay is stated clearly in the account.

The army travels to Tyriaeum and stays there for three days. It is reported that Epyaxa wants to see the army. Cyrus draws up the whole army on the plain.

The Greeks have their weapons. Every hoplite carries a shield, and the generals arrange their own contingents. Cyrus and Epyaxa observe the formation from vehicles.

The trumpet signals, and all the Greeks run toward the camp. Epyaxa is frightened and flees in her carriage. The people in the market leave their goods behind and flee.

The soldiers laugh, but the traders are afraid. The soldiers’ hands carry weapons, while the traders’ hands no longer hold their belongings. The same display appears impressive to some and frightening to others.

Later Epyaxa arrives at Tarsus before Cyrus. The army disrupts Cilicia, and the inhabitants are afraid. Syennesis does not approach Cyrus; but his wife persuades her husband. Syennesis receives assurances.

Syennesis and Cyrus come to discussions. One provides money for the army; the other gives gifts and makes promises concerning the country. Epyaxa does more than watch: she helps bring about the meeting. The account does not reveal the woman’s private intention.

Blue glosses support forms beyond the taught grammar; those untaught constructions are not assessed as morphology or production targets.

blocks.title: Words in the Reading
body: μισθός is wages; μισθὸς τεττάρων μηνῶν is wages for four months. Here μηνῶν identifies the amount of pay. It is not the accusative construction that says an action continues for a length of time.
γυνή can mean a woman or a wife. In ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ Συεννέσιος the relationship makes wife the appropriate translation; γυναικός reveals the stem used in most other cases.

πείθω means persuade; παρέχω means provide. Epyaxa’s role involves reported resources and an explicitly narrated act of persuasion. The words describe consequential action without assigning her an undocumented inner motive.

display.english: woman, wife / of a woman, wife

grammar.intro: Family -ρ- stems; γυνή and χείρ; πᾶς; cardinal numbers; time expressions. Work through each section, use its checks and topic practice, then complete the grammar exercises. Reading-only forms remain supported by glosses.
objectives: Recognize family-noun stem alternations in πατήρ, μήτηρ, and θυγάτηρ.
Decline γυνή and χείρ, including irregular dative plurals.
Use πᾶς for every, all, and the whole with appropriate agreement.
Read assigned cardinal numbers and inflect one, three, and four.
Distinguish when, duration, within-time, and quantities of wages in context.

sections.title: 1. Family Nouns in -ρ-
body: πατήρ, μήτηρ, and θυγάτηρ show stem alternation. The nominative has a long vowel, the accusative πατέρα/μητέρα/θυγατέρα keeps ε, and the genitive/dative singular lose ε: πατρός, πατρί; μητρός, μητρί; θυγατρός, θυγατρί.

Plural nominative and accusative use the ε-stem: πατέρες, πατέρας. Dative plural inserts α in πατράσι, μητράσι, θυγατράσι. Read these as learned noun patterns, not a command to drop ε from every ρ-stem.

Their gender comes from the dictionary article. ὁ πατήρ is masculine; ἡ μήτηρ and ἡ θυγάτηρ are feminine. An adjective must agree with that gender. These family nouns support a wider view of the people affected by an army even where the reading does not invent particular family scenes.

examples.english: He brings a gift to his father.

checks.prompt: Why are πατρός and πατέρα different stems?
checks.answer: The family-noun pattern drops ε in genitive/dative singular but retains it in accusative.

sections.title: 2. γυνή and χείρ
body: γυνή is irregular in its nominative; most forms use γυναικ-. Learn γυνή, γυναικός, ἡ together. The accusative is γυναῖκα; the dative γυναικί; the vocative γύναι. κ combines with σ in dative plural γυναιξί.

χείρ is feminine, even though its nominative shape resembles masculine models. It uses χειρ- in χειρός, χειρί, χεῖρα, and χεῖρες, but has χερσί in the dative plural. Its accent and stem behavior deserve direct attention.

The case system is unchanged: αἱ χεῖρες is subject plural; τὰς χεῖρας is object plural. The reading uses hands to contrast armed soldiers and traders losing hold of their goods. The comparison is adapted wording, not a preserved description of particular hands.

examples.english: He brings a gift to the woman.

checks.prompt: What is the gender of χείρ?

sections.title: 3. All, Every, and the Whole
body: πᾶς, πᾶσα, πᾶν has a third-declension παντ- pattern for masculine/neuter and a first-declension feminine. Nominative πᾶς and dative plural πᾶσι lose ντ before σ; genitive παντός reveals the stem.

Without the article, singular πᾶς στρατιώτης commonly means every soldier, treating members individually. With an article group, πᾶσα ἡ στρατιά means the whole army. Plural πάντες οἱ στρατιῶται means all the soldiers. Context matters; these examples supply the lesson’s controlled contrast.

The adjective agrees in gender, number, and case: πᾶσαν τὴν στρατιάν is feminine accusative singular; πάντας τοὺς στρατιώτας is masculine accusative plural. πᾶς placed inside an article group can have different nuances; today we focus on the clear every/all/whole patterns just shown.

examples.english: He draws up the whole army.

checks.prompt: How does πᾶσα ἡ στρατιά differ from πᾶς στρατιώτης?
checks.answer: The whole army as a unit versus every soldier individually.

sections.title: 4. Counting People, Days, and Months
body: Learn the cardinal sequence εἷς/μία/ἕν, δύο, τρεῖς/τρία, τέτταρες/τέτταρα, πέντε, ἕξ, ἑπτά, ὀκτώ, ἐννέα, δέκα. Also recognize εἴκοσι, twenty; ἑκατόν, a hundred; χίλιοι, a thousand. Five through ten, twenty, and a hundred do not decline; χίλιοι follows normal plural adjective agreement.

One has masculine, feminine, and neuter singular forms. Three and four have masculine/feminine forms and a distinct neuter: τρεῖς ἡμέραι but τρία δῶρα; τέτταρες μῆνες but τέτταρα ὅπλα. Their genitive/dative endings also change with case. δύο has the same nominative/accusative for all genders; the oblique form δυοῖν is supplied for recognition.

Numerals modify nouns with the case required by the construction. μισθὸς τεττάρων μηνῶν is four months’ wages, with genitive quantity; τρεῖς ἡμέρας μένει is he stays for three days, with accusative duration. Keep the number and the time noun together.

checks.prompt: Does πέντε change to agree with feminine ἡμέρας?
checks.answer: No. πέντε is indeclinable, though ἡμέρας still has case.

sections.title: 5. When, How Long, and Within What Time
body: Greek distinguishes three questions about time. A dative can say when: ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ, “on that day” (ἐκείνῃ means that). An accusative gives duration: τρεῖς ἡμέρας μένει, “he stays for three days.” A genitive gives the time within which something is accomplished: μιᾶς ἡμέρας τὴν ὁδὸν ποιοῦνται, “they complete the journey within one day.”

Context makes these meanings clearer than a bare case label. The within-time example supplies a completed journey inside a time window; it is not a general rule that every time genitive means within. The genitive can also express the part of time in which something happens, but our exercises focus on the three explicit constructions above.

The reading’s τεττάρων μηνῶν after μισθός gives a quantity of wages, not a time limit for completing an action. Compare μένει τέτταρας μῆνας, “he stays for four months.” The same real-world number can enter different constructions depending on what the sentence says.

table.title: Three time questions
rows: complete the journey within one day

examples.greek: ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τὸν μισθὸν δίδωσιν.
examples.english: On that day he gives the pay.

checks.prompt: What question does τρεῖς ἡμέρας answer after μένει?
checks.answer: How long does he stay? Three days.

summary.title: Grammar Summary
items: πατήρ/πατέρα but πατρός/πατρί; dative plural πατράσι.
γυνή uses γυναικ- in most cases; χείρ has irregular χερσί. Both are feminine.
πᾶς στρατιώτης is every soldier; πᾶσα ἡ στρατιά is the whole army; πάντες οἱ στρατιῶται is all the soldiers.
One, three, and four inflect; five through ten, twenty, and one hundred are fixed forms.
Dative can give when, accusative duration, genitive within-time. Genitive τεττάρων μηνῶν after μισθός instead gives quantity of pay.

sections.title: Resources and the status of a report
body: Anabasis 1.2.12 names Epyaxa as the wife of Syennesis, ruler of the Cilicians. Her arrival occurs while Cyrus owes the soldiers pay. Xenophon reports a story that she gave him substantial money and then states the payment of four months’ wages. The payment is firmer within his narrative than the reported explanation of where the money came from.

This distinction is a feature of the evidence, not a reason to remove Epyaxa from the story. Her presence and subsequent actions link finance with political relationships. Our adaptation avoids assigning her a speech or a hidden motive. It also avoids turning a reported financial transfer into independent proof about the exact origin of every coin paid to the troops.

sections.title: The army on display and the market in flight
body: At Tyriaeum Xenophon says that Epyaxa reportedly requested a review. Cyrus organizes the troops for display. The Greeks advance and then run toward their camp with a shout. Epyaxa flees in her vehicle, and people in the market abandon their wares. The soldiers’ laughter and Cyrus’s pleasure in the fear are part of the source’s uneven distribution of experience.

The review is impressive military coordination, but the same event terrifies people outside the formation. A market’s goods and the traders depending on them belong to the material story of war. Our adapted contrast of hands carrying weapons and hands losing goods makes this difference visible; that specific hand description is educational reconstruction.

sections.title: Negotiation and Cilicia’s vulnerability
body: The compressed continuation turns to Tarsus. Anabasis 1.2.25–27 records losses among Menon’s men, plundering in anger, and Syennesis’s reluctance to meet a more powerful figure. Epyaxa helps persuade her husband, and assurances are required before he meets Cyrus. The exact motives behind her decisions are not preserved in the account used here.

At the meeting Syennesis supplies money, and Cyrus gives prestigious gifts and promises concerning the land and captives. This follows harm to Cilicia; it is not a peaceful scene isolated from the army’s actions. Epyaxa acts within the political process, while civilians remain exposed to military pressure. Reflection should consider whose security a successful negotiation protects and whose losses remain.

questions.prompt: What distinction must be preserved about the money?
questions.answer: Epyaxa’s gift is reported; the four-month payment is stated in Xenophon’s account.

questions.prompt: Who is Epyaxa?
questions.answer: The wife of Syennesis, ruler of the Cilicians, and an actor in the expedition’s political relationships.

questions.prompt: Who reportedly requests the review?
How do people in the market react?
questions.answer: They flee and leave their goods behind.

questions.prompt: What role does Epyaxa play before the meeting with Syennesis?
questions.answer: She helps persuade him, and assurances are received before the meeting.

questions.prompt: What remains unknown about Epyaxa?
questions.answer: The account does not preserve her private intentions or exact words.
